chapter: Hurry On Down, Capitol and New York
title: Hurry On Down as a flat-fee hit
summary: Hurry On Down was recorded for a flat fee with a promised better contract, which manager Carlos Gastel later arranged.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Okay. When you were talking about your first recording and your test records -- was that what Dave Dexter called them, that he asked you to do?
Yes.

Then you recorded them, and you said among the numbers that you did in your first recording session for Capitol was, 'Hurry On Down,' and it was because of the success of those that you later got a better -- well, a better contract for which you had royalties. Does that mean that, 'Hurry On Down,' was your first hit, was it not?
Uh-huh. Uh-huh.
It became a hit and you had no royalties out of that hit?
Well --
Or did you?
At that time, when it became a hit, you know.
That was done for a flat fee?
It was done for a flat fee, with the understanding that I would have been given a better contract, see.
But whatever that made you didn't get anything.

Well, I don't recall getting -- I don't recall at that time getting it, but when I got a manager -- I did not have a manager at that time -- Carlos Gastel, when he came on the scene he changed all of that. He changed the contract and changed, you know, saw to it that I did get it.
Did you subsequently record, 'Hurry On
Down," again, or -- like when it appeared on the LP, that was the original?
That was the original. That's the original, "Hurry On Down."
So when it appeared on the LP did you then have a contract so that you got royalties?

Well, I don't know. I'll have to look into that. Because I'm thinking that Gastel. -- I was under the assumption that Gastel did get -- change the contract, because I was told if the thing is a hit we'll tear that contract up.
Oh.

That was the understanding, see. Because when I was approached to do a session for a flat fee, well naturally the first thing I thought, well, my God, -- not that I thought the thing would be a hit or anything. I wasn't thinking about that. But frankly, I had sort of lost some of my ambition at the time, to record, because I had -- you know, I had really strived so hard at the time to try to get on, you know, a label, and of course after it happened it was all to my benefit, because had I recorded prior to that, I probably would have recorded for a smaller label that wouldn't have -- would just have got lost in the shuffle somewhere, like those things do, you know.
Uh-huh.
So fortunately, it was worth my taking a chance, and then by me --
(End of proceedings as recorded.)
